skill_title: Define reaction rate, apply collision theory, and explain factors affecting rate
notes: 20 items: 4 lifted-style, 16 fresh. Reaction rate definition, collision theory (frequency, energy, orientation), factors: concentration, surface area, temperature, catalyst, pressure (gases).

items.question: Define REACTION RATE.
items.expectedAnswer: Reaction rate is the change in concentration of a reactant (decrease) or product (increase) per unit time, e.g. rate = −Δ[reactant]/Δt = +Δ[product]/Δt. SI unit: mol·dm⁻³·s⁻¹.
items.explanation: Rate = Δ[species]/Δt. Reactants: negative sign (consumed). Products: positive (formed). Always reported as positive.

items.question: State COLLISION THEORY of reaction rates.
items.expectedAnswer: For a reaction to occur, particles must COLLIDE with: (1) sufficient kinetic energy (≥ activation energy, Ea), AND (2) the correct ORIENTATION. Only such 'effective' collisions lead to products. The rate of reaction depends on the FREQUENCY of effective collisions.
items.explanation: Three requirements: collision (frequency) + sufficient energy (≥ Ea) + correct orientation. Effective collisions ⇒ reaction.

items.question: How does INCREASING THE CONCENTRATION of reactants affect the reaction rate? Explain using collision theory.
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing concentration INCREASES the rate. More particles per unit volume ⇒ more frequent collisions per unit time ⇒ more effective collisions per second ⇒ faster rate.
items.explanation: More particles → more collisions → more effective collisions per second → higher rate.

items.question: How does INCREASING the SURFACE AREA of a solid reactant affect the reaction rate?
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing surface area INCREASES the rate. More surface ⇒ more reactant particles exposed to the other reactant ⇒ more frequent collisions ⇒ faster rate. E.g. powdered solid reacts faster than the same mass as a single lump.
items.explanation: Powder > granules > lump. More surface area means more collision sites.

items.question: How does INCREASING the TEMPERATURE affect the reaction rate? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing T greatly INCREASES the rate. At higher T: (1) particles have more KE ⇒ collide more frequently AND (2) a LARGER FRACTION of particles have KE ≥ Ea ⇒ more effective collisions. The Ea-related effect dominates: typically rate doubles for every ~10°C increase.
items.explanation: T ↑ → both frequency ↑ AND fraction with KE ≥ Ea ↑. Rate goes up sharply.

items.question: What is the role of a CATALYST in a reaction? How does it affect the rate?
items.expectedAnswer: A catalyst provides an ALTERNATIVE REACTION PATHWAY with a LOWER activation energy (Ea). More particles can exceed the lower Ea ⇒ more effective collisions per second ⇒ faster rate. The catalyst is not consumed (regenerated at the end). It does NOT change ΔH or the equilibrium position, only the rate.
items.explanation: Catalyst: alternative pathway, lower Ea, faster rate. Doesn't change equilibrium or ΔH.

items.question: How does INCREASING the PRESSURE of a GASEOUS reaction affect the rate?
items.expectedAnswer: Increasing pressure (at constant T) compresses the gas, INCREASING the concentration (more particles per unit volume) ⇒ more frequent collisions ⇒ faster rate. For solids and liquids, pressure has negligible effect.
items.explanation: Pressure ↑ ⇒ effective [gas] ↑ ⇒ more collisions ⇒ faster.

items.question: What is ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea)?
items.expectedAnswer: Activation energy is the MINIMUM kinetic energy that colliding particles must have for a successful (effective) reaction to occur. It's the energy barrier between reactants and products. Below Ea, collisions bounce off without reacting.
items.explanation: Ea: minimum energy for reaction. Sets the 'threshold' for effective collisions.

items.question: A learner says: 'A catalyst increases the kinetic energy of the reactant particles.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. A catalyst does NOT change the kinetic energy of the particles (KE depends on temperature). A catalyst provides a LOWER-Ea pathway, so more particles can exceed Ea with their existing KE. The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is unchanged.
items.explanation: Catalyst lowers Ea, doesn't raise KE. Common misconception.

items.question: Why does breaking a solid into smaller pieces speed up its reaction with a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Breaking the solid into smaller pieces INCREASES its SURFACE AREA exposed to the liquid. More surface area ⇒ more contact between reactant particles ⇒ more frequent effective collisions per second ⇒ faster rate.
items.explanation: Powder = much more surface area than lump. More reactive surface = faster reaction.

items.question: A reaction takes 200 s at 25°C. At 35°C the same reaction (same amounts) takes about 100 s. Explain why.
items.expectedAnswer: At higher temperature, particles have MORE KE, so MORE particles exceed the activation energy. The fraction of effective collisions increases ⇒ the reaction proceeds faster ⇒ shorter time. The rule of thumb is that rate roughly doubles per 10°C increase, which fits this data.
items.explanation: T ↑ ⇒ exponentially more particles cross Ea ⇒ rate ↑. ~10°C ≈ ×2 rule.

items.question: What does the term EFFECTIVE COLLISION mean?
items.expectedAnswer: An effective collision is one that LEADS to a chemical reaction (i.e. forms products). The colliding particles must have KE ≥ Ea AND the correct orientation. Most collisions are NOT effective — they just bounce off.
items.explanation: Effective collision = enough energy AND correct orientation. Most collisions are ineffective.

items.question: A reaction: 2HCl(aq) + Mg(s) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Predict the EFFECT on the rate of (a) doubling [HCl]; (b) using Mg powder instead of a strip; (c) heating the system.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Doubles (or roughly doubles) the rate — more frequent collisions between HCl and Mg. (b) Increases the rate substantially — much greater surface area on Mg. (c) Increases the rate — higher KE, more particles above Ea.
items.explanation: Three factors: concentration, surface area, temperature. All increase rate when increased.

items.question: A learner says: 'Doubling the concentration of a reactant always doubles the rate.' Is this strictly correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Not strictly — it depends on the reaction order. If the reaction is FIRST ORDER in that reactant, doubling concentration doubles the rate. If SECOND order, doubling quadruples it. If ZERO order, no change. The qualitative direction (more concentration → faster) is right, but the exact factor depends on order. In CAPS, first-order behaviour is the usual assumption.
items.explanation: Rate ∝ [reactant]ⁿ. n = 1: doubles. n = 2: quadruples. n = 0: unchanged.

items.question: Two reactions with the same Ea proceed at different temperatures: 25°C and 45°C. At which temperature do MORE particles have KE ≥ Ea? Why?
items.expectedAnswer: At 45°C. Higher temperature ⇒ the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of KE shifts to higher energies AND broadens, so a larger fraction of particles have KE ≥ Ea. This is the main reason rate increases sharply with temperature.
items.explanation: T ↑: distribution shifts right, more particles past Ea ⇒ more effective collisions.

items.question: Sketch (or describe) the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures (T₁ < T₂) and indicate the activation energy Ea.
items.expectedAnswer: Description: Both curves are bell-shaped, peaking and tailing off at high KE. At higher T₂: the curve is BROADER (shifted to the right and flatter). Mark Ea on the x-axis. The AREA UNDER the curve to the right of Ea represents the fraction of particles with KE ≥ Ea — larger area at T₂ than T₁.
items.explanation: Maxwell-Boltzmann: shifts right and broadens at higher T. Fraction past Ea increases.

items.question: Explain WHY a CATALYST does NOT change the EQUILIBRIUM position.
items.expectedAnswer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of BOTH the forward AND the reverse reactions by the SAME amount. So it increases both rates equally, leaving the equilibrium constant Kc and the equilibrium concentrations unchanged. It only accelerates the approach TO equilibrium.
items.explanation: Catalyst lowers Ea equally on both sides. Same Kc, same equilibrium position, just faster to get there.

items.question: Which of the following will NOT affect the reaction rate?
options: Increasing the concentration of a reactant
Adding more of an inert gas at constant volume (gas-phase reaction)
items.expectedAnswer: Adding more of an inert gas at constant volume (gas-phase reaction)
items.explanation: Inert gas at constant V doesn't change partial pressure/concentration of reactants. No effect on rate.

items.question: Why does combustion of paper burn faster when the paper is shredded vs. as a single sheet?
items.expectedAnswer: Shredded paper has much greater surface area exposed to oxygen. More surface area ⇒ more contact between paper (fuel) and O₂ (reactant) ⇒ more collisions per second ⇒ faster combustion. (Same reason flour dust can explode but a flour bag won't.)
items.explanation: Surface area effect again. Powders/finely divided solids react MUCH faster than bulk.

items.question: List THREE factors that can be changed to INCREASE the rate of a reaction.
items.expectedAnswer: Any three of: (1) Increase concentration of reactants (or pressure for gases); (2) Increase temperature; (3) Increase surface area of solids (e.g. powder vs lump); (4) Add a catalyst; (5) Increase intensity of light (for photochemical reactions).
items.explanation: Five typical factors. CAPS expects four main ones (concentration, T, surface area, catalyst).

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COLLISION_THEORY_INCOMPLETE: Misses orientation or Ea in collision theory
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RATE_CONCENTRATION: Wrong direction of concentration effect on rate
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COLLISION_FREQUENCY: Doesn't link concentration to collision frequency
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RATE_SURFACE_AREA: Wrong direction of surface area effect
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_T_VS_EA: Doesn't link temperature to fraction past Ea
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RATE_PRESSURE: Wrong direction of pressure effect on gas rate
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_EFFECTIVE_COLLISION: Wrong definition of effective collision (orientation + energy)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_REACTION_ORDER: Confuses qualitative rate increase with linear/quadratic order
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_MAXWELL_BOLTZMANN: Wrong description of M-B distribution shift with T
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_INERT_GAS_RATE: Wrong effect of inert gas on rate
